title: Closures Of Convex Functions
notes: Open by making the epigraph the protagonist. Convexity supplies the shape, but closedness decides whether limiting boundary points are part of the function. The lecture will keep returning to the same move: close the epigraph, then read the repaired lower boundary as the closed hull.

title: Epigraph Closure
notes: Use the picture to separate graph intuition from epigraph intuition. The graph may look like a horizontal ray, but the mathematical object is the filled region above it. Closing that region inserts the missing endpoint and lowers the boundary value there without changing any interior sample.

title: Lower Semicontinuity
notes: Lower semicontinuity is the no downward surprise condition. If a sequence approaches x, the value at x must not sit above the limiting lower envelope. The useful theorem is that this analytic statement, closed sublevel sets, and closed epigraphs are three views of the same condition.

title: Boundary Limit Values
notes: Now specialize to a proper convex function and pick an anchor in the relative interior of the domain. Moving from the anchor toward any boundary point gives a one-dimensional convex trace. The closure value at the endpoint is the ordinary radial limit along that trace.

title: Closed Hull Operation
notes: The closed hull is not a smoothing algorithm and it is not a pointwise average. It is a geometric projection of the closed epigraph back to a function. That is why cl f is below f, has the same infimum, and changes values only where the epigraph had missing boundary.

title: Proper Functions
notes: Pause on properness because it prevents two misleading edge cases. A proper convex function has a nonempty finite domain and no minus infinity values. Under closure it remains proper and agrees on the relative interior; functions that hit minus infinity belong to the special improper branch.

title: Indicator And Support Examples
notes: Indicators and support functions are a useful contrast. The indicator of an open convex set visibly changes when closure adds boundary points. A support function already takes suprema of continuous linear probes, so replacing a set by its closure leaves the support values unchanged.

title: Discontinuous Convex Example
notes: This is the smallest example where the operation has teeth. The function is zero on the open ray and infinite at the endpoint, so convexity alone does not force lower semicontinuity. Closing the epigraph adds exactly one endpoint value and leaves the rest of the ray alone.

title: Closure And Conjugacy Preview
notes: Do not develop conjugacy yet, but show why this section is not an isolated technicality. The conjugate sees supporting affine functions, and the biconjugate later returns the closed convex representative. The closure convention is chosen so that this duality statement keeps working cleanly.

title: Slices Of Epigraphs
notes: Horizontal slices translate epigraph geometry into level-set geometry. For levels above the infimum, the closed slice is controlled by cl f, while the relative interior of the slice is obtained by strict inequality inside the relative interior of the domain. This is a practical theorem for inequalities.

title: Numerical Lsc Check
notes: The ledger is intentionally modest: it does not prove every sequence, but it catches the designed boundary defect. Sampling x_k equal to one over k gives values tending to zero. The original endpoint value fails the lsc inequality; the closed hull endpoint value passes it.

title: Failure Modes
notes: Use this as the guardrail slide. A closed function need not have a closed domain, and repairing a formula by hand is not the same as closing its epigraph. The level-set relative-interior formulas also need convexity; similar-looking nonconvex functions can defeat them.

title: Rule Ledger
notes: Read the ledger as a proof checklist rather than as a list of slogans. Each rule tells the instructor which object to inspect: sequences, epigraphs, relative interiors, radial traces, or level slices. The recurring diagnostic is whether a suspected defect lives on the relative boundary.

title: Recap
notes: Close by asking students to narrate the whole operation from memory. Start with a convex function, move to its epigraph, close the epigraph, read the new lower boundary, and then check properness, relative-interior agreement, boundary values, and level-set slices before using the function downstream.
